title: ‘Your Excel Skills Suck’: The Power Users Turning Spreadsheets Into a Spectator Sport
gist: A community of Excel 'power user' influencers has turned spreadsheet speedruns and obstacle courses into a viral creator-economy niche with hundreds of thousands of followers and an official world championship, and several insist AI won't beat their manual dexterity.

insights.claim: Excel 'power user' influencers have built large short-form video followings (300,000+ combined for individual creators) by turning enterprise spreadsheet software into speedrun and obstacle-course content, showing that even ostensibly boring B2B software topics can achieve mainstream viral reach.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Signals durable demand for skill-based short-form content and creator monetization even in narrow enterprise-software niches, relevant to platforms building creator tools around productivity software.

insights.claim: A single viral Excel speedrun clip posted by creator Dan Kidney reached 1 million views within days, and his TikTok/Instagram accounts have grown to a combined 300,000 followers, illustrating how quickly niche productivity content can scale on short-form platforms.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of virality velocity for niche B2B-adjacent content, useful for gauging creator-platform engagement dynamics outside typical entertainment categories.
insights.locator: A few weeks in, Kidney posted footage of himself racing through

insights.claim: The Microsoft Excel World Championships have become a recognized competitive esport with international contestants (Diarmuid Early of Ireland won 2025 in Las Vegas; Andrew Ngai of Australia won three consecutive prior titles 2021-2023), indicating spreadsheet mastery now supports prize-money competition and audience engagement similar to niche esports.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: An underexploited esports/spectator-content adjacency (sponsorships, ticketed streams) exists around productivity software mastery, comparable to how chess and typing competitions became monetizable spectator content.

insights.claim: Finance-influencer Jonathan Tristan, a former investment banker with roughly 700,000 followers, markets keyboard-only Excel efficiency to Wall Street audiences by framing incremental speed gains (10% faster) as directly trading off against sleep hours worked in 10-hour Excel days.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Reflects a hustle-culture content angle that finance-adjacent influencer audiences reward efficiency messaging tied explicitly to work-hour and burnout economics.
insights.quote: going 10 percent faster if you spend 10 hours a day in Excel, he says, is the difference between “getting five hours of sleep versus six hours of sleep.”
insights.locator: Tristan, who has shared his own impressive Excel speedruns

themes.theme: AI substitution skepticism among domain experts

insights.claim: Excel speedrunner Ryan Park dismisses claims that AI could complete his tasks faster, arguing he'd finish a task manually before someone could even finish explaining the desired outcome to an AI tool, and separately predicts Excel is not going obsolete, comparing it to pen and paper.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Domain-expert skepticism toward AI substitution claims in a routine white-collar task is a useful data point for gauging real-world AI adoption friction versus hype, especially where human dexterity remains visibly competitive.
insights.quote: My response is that I’d be done before they can even explain the desired outcome to an AI tool
insights.locator: Park, for one, brushes off replies about Excel being “so 20 years ago”

insights.claim: Ryan Park predicts Excel will remain foundational business infrastructure indefinitely despite the rise of AI tools, comparing the idea of its obsolescence to claiming pen and paper will disappear.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: A useful counterweight to narratives of imminent AI displacement of spreadsheet-based workflows in enterprise software.
insights.quote: It’s like saying that pen and paper will be obsolete,
insights.locator: As for Excel itself, Park doesn’t believe it’s going anywhere

insights.claim: Independent creators are building standalone tutorial businesses around Excel mastery, including Drew Koontz's Encyclopedia Excel and George Lungu's Excel Unusual (which showcases flight simulators, physics engines, and roller coasters built entirely in Excel), and Ryan Park's gamified paid obstacle-course product that he says has helped 'tens of thousands' of users.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Indicates white-space for platforms bundling gamification, tutorial monetization, and community features around mastery of specific enterprise software products.
insights.locator: According to Koontz, speed is far from the only way
